title: A King's Dream of Falling Kingdoms
overview: When Babylon's king demands that someone tell him his own dream, Daniel receives it from God and explains that the kingdoms pictured in a great statue will fall, while a kingdom set up by God will last forever.

parts.label: The king's impossible demand (vv. 1-13)
parts.note: Nebuchadnezzar insists his advisers tell him the dream itself, not just its meaning, as proof they are not simply making things up. When they admit only the gods could do that, he orders every wise man in Babylon killed, and the guards come looking for Daniel and his friends too.

parts.label: Daniel prays with friends (vv. 14-23)
parts.note: Daniel tactfully asks for time and urges his three friends to pray with him for mercy, and the dream is shown to him that night. His song of thanks praises God as the one who removes kings, sets up others, and brings hidden things to light.

parts.label: Daniel tells the dream (vv. 24-35)
parts.note: Daniel stops the executions and tells the king plainly that no human skill found this, only a God in heaven who reveals secrets. The dream was a huge statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, shattered by a stone cut out without human hands that grew into a mountain filling the earth.

parts.label: The four kingdoms explained (vv. 36-43)
parts.note: The gold head is Nebuchadnezzar himself, followed by a lesser kingdom, a bronze one, and an iron kingdom that crushes the others yet ends up divided, like iron mixed with clay. Older readers often saw Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, while many modern scholars see Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, with the iron and clay as Greek kingdoms that stayed split despite royal marriages.

parts.label: A kingdom no one can end (vv. 44-45)
parts.note: The stone stands for a kingdom God himself sets up, which will crush the kingdoms of the statue and never be destroyed or handed to another people. Christians have read this stone as pointing to Jesus and the kingdom he announced.

parts.label: The king honors Daniel (vv. 46-49)
parts.note: Nebuchadnezzar bows to Daniel, orders offerings made to him, and declares Daniel's God to be God over gods and Lord over kings. He gives Daniel high office over Babylon and, at Daniel's request, promotes his three friends as well.

disagreement: Christians differ over which empires the four metals represent and whether God's kingdom, pictured by the stone, already arrived with Jesus or still lies mainly in the future.
think: When a ruler or system seems unshakable, what do you think actually decides whether it lasts?
